extracted.intended_audience: Area Chairs (ACs) for ICLR 2025 / program committee members
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for Area Chairs handling paper assignment, discussion moderation, reviewer management, and writing meta-reviews / accept-reject recommendations for ICLR 2025 submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewing Process Manager duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Help the Program Chairs manage the reviewing process: recommend appropriate reviewers, and when reviewers are delinquent or not responsive, assign alternate reviewers in a timely manner so every submission gets a chance to be judged fairly and expertly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may skip recommending reviewers (the system can assign based on profiles), but ACs should vet/recommend reviewer assignments, identify delinquent reviewers and assign alternates. The program expects ~3 quality reviews per paper. When reviewers are unresponsive after the review deadline, immediately start looking for and recruiting an emergency reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision maker responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: For every submission, recommend whether it should be accepted or rejected and accompany the recommendation with a meta-review summarizing reviews and discussion and optionally adding your own view of the paper's merits and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AC recommendation is non-binding; Senior Area Chairs and Program Chairs will help. Flag papers for desk reject when appropriate. Watch for reviewers' flags for Code of Ethics violations — collect information and evidence and provide it. ACs should engage with reviewers to reach an informed decision and may consult SACs/PCs when unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review length expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim to write a meta-review of at least 60 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs have full freedom in writing meta-reviews, but authors find meta-reviews useful when they meet this minimum length and include suggested elements (see other meta-review items).

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: concise description of submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a concise description of the submission’s main content (scientific claims and findings), based on your own reading and reviewers’ characterization, including the paper’s strengths and weaknesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideally the description should contain both what is discussed in the submission and what is missing from the submission. This helps authors understand the AC's view of the paper's contributions and gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: concise summary of discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize the discussion: list the points raised by the reviewers, how each point was addressed by the authors, and whether the AC found each point worth consideration in decision making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICLR provides many weeks of discussion; ACs are encouraged to reflect that discussion in the meta-review. If virtual reviewer-AC meetings occurred for borderline papers, summarize those meeting outcomes and post them on OpenReview.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meta-review: recommendation and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: End the meta-review with a clear indication of your recommendation (accept/reject) and a justification based on the content and discussion of the submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The recommendation must be justified using the points described above (paper content, reviewers' points, authors' responses, and meeting outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion moderation (tone and scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderate the discussion to keep it focused on scientific merits, limitations, and clarifications, discouraging participation that is irrelevant or toxic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the language used in reviews and meta-reviews is constructive and polite. Discourage participation in any discussion that is irrelevant to scientific claims. Identify and respond to Code of Ethics violations during discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage reviewer engagement with authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage reviewers to respond to author rebuttals and to participate actively in the discussion so that authors receive useful feedback and clarifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs should actively engage with assigned reviewers and authors when a submission does not receive the attention it deserves; ask for clarifications or arguments as needed to judge contributions fairly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion participant role (scientific expertise)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in discussions with your own expert view of the paper and ask authors (or any commentator) for clarifications when needed to understand and judge contributions fairly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs were invited because of their expertise and reputation — their assessment is a critical factor in decision making. Be an active participant, not just a moderator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize virtual reviewer-AC meetings for borderline papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Required to organize one virtual AC/reviewer meeting for each borderline paper and summarize discussions from the meeting and post it in OpenReview.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetings are primarily for borderline papers; historically this is 3–4 papers per AC. ACs are encouraged to also discuss meta-reviews with SACs via virtual meetings for cases they are unsure of.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and identification of borderline papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Borderline papers will be identified primarily using review scores and the spread of scores; this will be used as a proxy to catch most borderline papers among many submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs also have the right to organize meetings for any other papers they consider borderline/worth discussing. The program will notify ACs which papers fall into the borderline bucket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer meeting logistics and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: When organizing meetings, collect reviewer emails visible on OpenReview, use scheduling tools (e.g., doodle), consider time zones, provide an online meeting tool (e.g., Jitsi), and ask reviewers to be prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a majority of reviewers do not attend, send reminders, escalate to SACs if needed, and proceed with the meeting if necessary. Note reviewers who fail to attend will be marked for future reference (excluding emergencies). ACs may downweight reviews of reviewers who refuse to attend meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling non-responsive reviewers and emergency/additional reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek emergency/additional reviewers in two cases: assigned reviewers are unresponsive after the review deadline, or additional reviews could improve confidence in your recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a review was not submitted by the deadline and the paper lacks 3 informed reviews, immediately start finding an emergency reviewer. Assign emergency reviewers via links in the AC console. If you struggle, contact the Senior AC or program chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: When and how to assign emergency/additional reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the AC console to assign emergency reviewers; contact SACs or program chairs if you cannot find a reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This step is important for timely feedback to authors and to ensure fair judging. Emergency reviewers should be recruited promptly when reviewers are delinquent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to direct author messages
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may message their corresponding ACs via OpenReview comments. ACs are expected to respond to reasonable inquiries promptly and escalate to SACs if the question requires further discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These comments are often used to flag concerns or to activate discussions; treat them as part of the discussion moderation responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling author revisions during discussion
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may revise their submission up until Nov 27; final decisions and meta-reviews should take revisions into account, but ACs may ignore a revision if it is substantially different from the original version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of the revision timeline and consider whether revisions materially affect your recommendation; explicit permission is given to ignore substantially different revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of Ethics handling and escalation
rubrics_metrics.description: All participants must adhere to the Code of Ethics. If submissions/reviews/comments raise ethical concerns, flag problematic content, collect information/evidence, and contact the Program Chairs. Flagged papers may be passed to the Ethics Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The AC's recommendation regarding ethics-flagged papers is non-binding; collect evidence (from paper, discussion with authors/reviewers) and provide it. If in doubt, consult SACs or Program Chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure reviewer judgments align with ICLR reviewer guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure reviewers’ judgments are in line with the ICLR 2025 reviewer guidelines and pay attention to related FAQs (e.g., definition of contemporaneous work for citations and empirical comparisons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer reviewers to the Reviewer Guide and its FAQs; ACs should enforce alignment and help calibrate reviewers when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contemporaneous work and citation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are expected to cite and discuss very recent work; 'contemporaneous' is defined as published within the last four months. Authors are encouraged to cite non peer-reviewed works (e.g., arXiv) but may be excused for not knowing about papers not published in peer-reviewed venues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ACs should use the FAQ guidance when judging whether omissions are reasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision basis and calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: Base your accept/reject recommendations on the reviews and the quality of the papers rather than fitting to a rating curve, which will not be shared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SACs will help calibrate if needed. The goal of ICLR is to accept quality papers without being constrained to a pre-shared curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the stated timeline for AC duties (assignment confirmations, review periods, chasing late reviews, discussion windows, meta-review deadlines, author notification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key dates were provided (e.g., review period, discussion period, meta-review due dates). ACs are expected to chase late reviews, organize meetings in a timely fashion, and meet meta-review deadlines (meta reviews due end of discussion stage timeline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and civility
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure that the language used in reviews and AC meta-reviews is constructive, polite, and non-toxic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer reviewers to advice such as 'Criticizing with Kindness' and other suggested reading for constructive review writing. Moderate discussions to enforce civility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and transparency (OpenReview posting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summaries of reviewer meetings and discussion outcomes should be posted to OpenReview so that the public discussion forum for the submission reflects AC moderation and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When summarizing meetings, include the points raised and outcomes so authors and the community can see how the decision was reached.
